claim: The Arabidopsis genome encodes six TIR1/AFB proteins representing three of the four clades that were established prior to angiosperm radiation.
source: The Arabidopsis genome encodes six TIR1/AFB proteins representing three of the four clades that were established prior to angiosperm radiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of all six TIR1/AFB proteins results in early embryo defects and eventually seed abortion.
source: We find that loss of all six TIR1/AFB proteins results in early embryo defects and eventually seed abortion
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by embryo imaging data in Figure 3.

claim: A single wild-type allele of TIR1 or AFB2 is sufficient to support growth throughout development.
source: and yet a single wild-type allele of TIR1 or AFB2 is sufficient to support growth throughout development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by the viability of tir1/+ afb12345 and afb2/+ tir1afb1345 plants shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is extensive functional overlap between even the most distantly related TIR1/AFB genes except for AFB1.
source: Our analysis reveals extensive functional overlap between even the most distantly related TIR1/AFB genes except for AFB1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the genetic analysis of all 63 mutant combinations.

claim: AFB1 has a specialized function in rapid auxin-dependent inhibition of root growth and early phase of root gravitropism.
source: Surprisingly, AFB1 has a specialized function in rapid auxin-dependent inhibition of root growth and early phase of root gravitropism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 6 and 7.

claim: AFB1's specialized activity may be related to a difference in subcellular localization compared to the other members of the family.
source: This activity may be related to a difference in subcellular localization compared to the other members of the family.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by fluorescence quantification data in Figure 5S showing AFB1-mCitrine is primarily cytoplasmic.

claim: Three clades of auxin receptors were established prior to the radiation of euphyllophytes (ferns plus seed plants) over 400 million years ago.
source: While the last common ancestors of land plants and of vascular plants had only one TIR1/AFB gene, three clades of auxin receptors were established prior to the radiation of euphyllophytes (ferns plus seed plants) over 400 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, with citation to Morris et al., 2018.

claim: AFB6 orthologs are not present in the genomes of core Brassicales species including Arabidopsis, nor those of Poaceae species including rice and maize.
source: For example, AFB6 orthologs are not present in the genomes of core Brassicales species—including Arabidopsis—nor those of Poaceae species including rice and maize.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The gene duplication event establishing the distinct TIR1 and AFB1 clades is coincident with the At-β WGD event at the base of Brassicales.
source: The gene duplication event establishing the distinct TIR1 and AFB1 clades is coincident with the At-β WGD event at the base of Brassicales, while both the AFB2/AFB3 and the AFB4/AFB5 duplication events coincide with the more recent At-α WGD prior to divergence of the Brassicaceae family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006.

claim: Since the last common ancestor of Arabidopsis and Tarenaya, the AFB1 gene has accumulated over three times as many non-synonymous changes as TIR1.
source: Since the last common ancestor of Arabidopsis (Brassicaceae) and Tarenaya (Cleomaceae), the AFB1 gene has accumulated over three times as many non-synonymous changes as TIR1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by branch length data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AFB1 is under selection based on the ratio of non-synonymous and synonymous substitutions.
source: despite being under selection based on the ratio of non-synonymous and synonymous substitutions (Delker et al., 2010; Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Delker et al., 2010 and Wright et al., 2017.

claim: AFB1 contains two of three substitutions in the first α-helix of the F-Box that were each previously shown to weaken TIR1's interaction with CUL1.
source: AFB1 also differs from the other TIR1/AFBs in that it contains two of three substitutions in the first α-helix of the F-Box that were each previously shown to weaken TIR1's interaction with CUL1 (Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Yu et al., 2015.

claim: The Glu8Lys substitution in AFB1 appeared shortly after the At-β WGD that produced AFB1.
source: The substitution with the largest effect, Glu8Lys (equivalent to Glu12Lys in TIR1), appeared shortly after the At-β WGD that produced AFB1, and the Phe14Leu substitution appeared prior to the crown group of the Brassicaceae family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by phylogenetic data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The tir1-1 allele does not act as a dominant-negative allele.
source: However, we found that the root elongation phenotype of plants heterozygous for the tir1-1, tir1-10, and tir1-9 alleles were not significantly different from each other and each displays a semi-dominant phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B). These results argue against a dominant negative effect for tir1-1 since neither tir1-9 or tir1-10 produce detectable levels of transcript (Ruegger et al., 1998; Parry et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, with citations to Ruegger et al., 1998 and Parry et al., 2009.

claim: The sixty-three mutant combinations displayed a wide range of phenotypes from indistinguishable from wild type to early-embryo lethality.
source: The sixty-three mutant combinations displayed a wide range of phenotypes from indistinguishable from wild type to early-embryo lethality (Figure 1—figure supplement 3; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The three viable quintuple mutants—tir1afb1245, tir1afb1345, and afb12345—had rosettes approximately half the diameter and inflorescences less than half the height of WT Col-0.
source: The three viable quintuple mutants—tir1afb1245, tir1afb1345, and afb12345—had rosettes approximately half the diameter and inflorescences less than half the height of WT Col-0.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by measurements in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Lines retaining only one copy of TIR1 (tir1/+ afb12345) or one copy of AFB2 (afb2/+ tir1afb1345) were viable.
source: Remarkably, lines retaining only one copy of TIR1 (tir1/+ afb12345) or one copy of AFB2 (afb2/+ tir1afb1345) were viable.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The afb2/+ tir1afb1345 and tir1/+ afb12345 plants rarely produced seeds.
source: The afb2/+ tir1afb1345 and tir1/+ afb12345 plants rarely produced seeds.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observation of the plants.

claim: 32% of tir1afb1245 siliques have only one valve.
source: Normal siliques (Col-0, left) have two valves containing developing seeds while 32% of tir1afb1245 siliques have only one.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1C caption and shown in the image.

claim: The tir1 mutation had the largest effect on root elongation inhibition by auxin.
source: For both the root elongation assay and the induction of lateral root primordia, the tir1 allele had the largest effect with the afb2, afb5, afb3, and afb4 mutations having smaller median effects (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation.
source: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation but, surprisingly, had an opposite effect on lateral root formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The afb1 mutation had an opposite effect on lateral root formation compared to other TIR1/AFB mutations.
source: The afb1 mutation had little or no effect on root elongation but, surprisingly, had an opposite effect on lateral root formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The afb1 mutation suppressed the lateral root phenotype of the afb234 triple mutant.
source: We found that the afb1 mutation suppressed the phenotype of both the afb234 (2.15 ± 0.13 versus 1.75 ± 0.10 lateral roots/cm) and afb345 triple mutants (3.10 ± 0.13 versus 1.96 ± 0.14 lateral roots/cm) measured after 12 days on media not supplemented with IAA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific measurements provided.

claim: The afb2345 quadruple mutant is over 6 cm smaller in rosette diameter than each of the four triple mutants.
source: However, they have huge collective effects, where the afb2345 quadruple mutant is over 6 cm smaller than each of the four triple mutants (blue arrowheads; Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and indicated in Figure 2C.

claim: The afb5 mutation has the largest effect on inflorescence branching and height.
source: Consistent with previous reports that AFB5 plays a key role in regulating inflorescence branching and height (Prigge et al., 2016; Ligerot et al., 2017), the afb5 mutation has the largest effect on these phenotypes, although each mutation, except for afb1, had some effect (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Prigge et al., 2016 and Ligerot et al., 2017, and shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: The penetrance of the rootless seedling phenotype for tir1afb23, tir1afb123, and tir1afb245 lines was significantly lower at 20°C than at either 17°C or 23°C.
source: The penetrance of the phenotype for all three lines was significantly lower at 20°C than at either 17°C or 23°C for all with the exception that the difference with tir1afb245 at 17°C was not significant using the Fisher's exact test.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: Aspects of the auxin regulatory system are sensitive to temperature.
source: This suggests that aspects of the auxin regulatory system are sensitive to temperature.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the temperature-dependent penetrance data.

claim: Approximately one-quarter of embryos from tir1/+ afb235 or afb2/+ tir1afb35 plants lacked cotyledons and had over-proliferated suspensors.
source: Eleven of 41 (27%) and 52 of 213 (24%), respectively, of the embryos from each line lacked cotyledons and had over-proliferated suspensors while the rest had a WT phenotype (Figure 3A, A').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 3A, A'.

claim: The initial division of the embryo proper was occasionally displaced from vertical in sextuple mutant 2-cell embryos compared to complemented siblings.
source: The earliest potential difference between sextuple mutants and the complemented siblings is that the initial division of the embryo proper was occasionally displaced from vertical in sextuple 2-cell embryos (3 of 19 were >12° from vertical) compared to complemented sibling embryos (0 of 64), however the average angles from vertical were not significantly different (p=0.32) (Figure 3B–C versus 3B′–C′, 3N).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 3B-C, B'-C', and 3N.

claim: The curvature of the lower surface of the upper tier in 8-cell embryos is significantly more prominent in sextuple mutants than in complemented siblings.
source: The third round of divisions in the embryo proper separates the upper and lower tiers with the lower surface of the upper tier typically being slightly convex, and this curvature is significantly more prominent in the sextuple mutants (p=1.4 × 10−7; Figure 3D versus 3D′, 3O).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical significance and shown in Figure 3D, D', and 3O.

claim: 69% of cell divisions during the transition from 8-cell to 16-cell embryos are anticlinal in sextuple mutant embryos, compared to nearly all being periclinal in complemented embryos.
source: Later, during the transition from the 8-cell to the 16-cell embryos, nearly all cell divisions in the complemented embryos are oriented periclinally, as in WT embryos. In contrast, 69% of these division are anticlinal in the mutant embryos (Figure 3E and E', 3P).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E, E', and 3P.

claim: The asymmetric division of the hypophysis cell was delayed in sextuple mutant embryos and when it occurred, was symmetrical.
source: In WT 32-cell stage embryos, the hypophysis cell normally divides asymmetrically to produce the lens-shaped cell which is required for the formation of the embryonic root. This division was delayed in the mutant, and when it occurred, was symmetrical (Figure 3G–H and 3G′–H′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3G-H and G'-H'.

claim: Cells of the sextuple mutant embryo proper slow or cease dividing and the cells of the suspensor begin to proliferate.
source: Later, the cells of the embryo proper slow or cease dividing and the cells of the suspensor begin to proliferate and invariably produce a radially symmetric terminal phenotype (Figure 3I–M, 3I′–M′).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3I-M and I'-M'.

claim: Around the bent-cotyledon stage, the cells of the sextuple mutant senesce and seed development is aborted.
source: Around the stage where complemented siblings are at the bent-cotyledon stage, the cells of the sextuple mutant senesce and seed development is aborted (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The sextuple mutant reveals the importance of TIR1/AFB auxin response machinery from the earliest stages of embryogenesis.
source: Hence, the sextuple mutant reveals the importance of TIR1/AFB auxin response machinery from the earliest stages of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the embryo phenotype data.

claim: Expression of the auxin-responsive marker DR5rev:3×Venus-N7 was undetectable in tir1afb235 quadruple mutant embryos.
source: Expression of the auxin-responsive marker DR5rev:3×Venus-N7 was undetectable in embryos displaying the mutant phenotype (Figure 4E–G; compare to Figure 4A–C; 0/10 in quadruple mutants and 26/26 in non-mutant siblings) indicating that auxin-regulated transcription through the remaining receptors, AFB4 and AFB1, is minimal at most during embryogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4E-G compared to 4A-C.

claim: The quiescent center marker WOX5:GFP was not detected in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
source: Similarly, the quiescent center marker WOX5:GFP was not detected in the mutant embryos (Figure 4H), whereas in wild type the reporter is first expressed in the hypophysis prior to its asymmetric division then persists in the quiescent center cells (Figure 4D; 0/11 in quadruple mutants and 28/28 in non-mutant siblings).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4H compared to 4D.

claim: PIN7-Venus signal is much stronger in protodermal cells of the embryo proper in tir1afb235 mutant embryos compared to wild type.
source: In mutant embryos, PIN7-Venus is faintly detectable in these cells in globular-stage embryos. Unexpectedly, the signal is much stronger in protodermal cells of the embryo proper, especially in the lower tier, by the 32-cell stage (Figure 4O–P; 7/8 quadruple mutants and 0/14 siblings).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4O-P.

claim: PIN1-Venus signal is reduced and restricted primarily to apical protodermal cells in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
source: In the mutants, PIN1-Venus signal is reduced and restricted primarily to apical protodermal cells (Figure 4M–N; 9/9 quadruple mutants).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4M-N.

claim: NTT-YPet is progressively lost in the distal suspensor cells before abnormal lateral cell divisions occur in tir1afb235 mutant embryos.
source: In mutants, NTT-YPet appears normally in most suspensor cells, but not always including the hypophysis (2/6 32-cell quadruple mutant embryos had signal above background in the hypophysis), and is progressively lost in the distal suspensor cells before the abnormal lateral cell divisions occur (Figure 4V–X; 4/4 late-globular-stage mutants lacked signal in both the hypophysis and the adjacent suspensor cell).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific counts and shown in Figure 4V-X.

claim: Gametophytically-expressed TIR1/AFBs do not contribute to gametophytic viability.
source: This indicates that gametophytically expressed TIR1/AFBs do not contribute to gametophytic viability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on transmission rate data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The sextuple mutant was transmitted nearly as well without the complementing transgene as with it through both the pollen (49.4%) and the female gametophyte (47.9%).
source: The sextuple mutant was transmitted nearly as well as without the complementing transgene as with it through both the pollen (49.4%) and the female gametophyte (47.9%) (χ2 test p=0.81 and 0.43, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with specific percentages and statistical tests.

claim: AFB5-mCitrine fluorescent signal was fairly uniformly distributed in shoot apices.
source: The fluorescent signal in the AFB5-mCitrine lines was fairly uniformly distributed in shoot apices (Figure 5F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5F.

claim: In AFB3-mCitrine, AFB2-mCitrine, and TIR1-mCitrine lines, fluorescence was more restricted to young primordia and meristem peripheral zones.
source: while in the AFB3-mCitrine, AFB2-mCitrine, and TIR1-mCitrine lines, fluorescence was more restricted to young primordia and meristem peripheral zones (Figure 5A and C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5A, C-D.

claim: TIR1-mCitrine appears to be strongest in the adaxial domains of the youngest primordia.
source: Within organ primordia, TIR1-mCitrine appears to be strongest in the adaxial domains of the youngest primordia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on observation of fluorescence patterns.

claim: Signal for the AFB4-mCitrine line was barely detectable.
source: Signal for the AFB4-mCitrine line was barely detectable (Figure 5E)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: AFB1-mCitrine signal was very strong and largely complementary to TIR1-mCitrine, with the strongest signal in abaxial domains and in the stem.
source: while that of AFB1-mCitrine was very strong and largely complementary to TIR1-mCitrine in that the strongest signal was in abaxial domains and in the stem (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine signal was uniformly detected throughout the root meristematic region and fainter signal detected in the root cap cells.
source: TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine signal was uniformly detected throughout the root meristematic region and fainter signal detected in the root cap cells (Figure 5G, I–J and L; Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5G, I-J, L and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: AFB1-mCitrine is very highly expressed throughout the root except for the columella, cortex, endodermis, and pericycle of the meristematic region.
source: AFB1-mCitrine is very highly expressed throughout the root except for the columella, cortex, endodermis, and pericycle of the meristematic region (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5H.

claim: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors.
source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claim: AFB4-mCitrine's signal in embryos was close to background levels.
source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claim: AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable in embryos.
source: In embryos, TIR1-, AFB2-, AFB3-, and AFB5-mCitrine accumulate fairly uniformly throughout the embryos and suspensors while AFB4-mCitrine's signal was close to background levels and AFB1-mCitrine was undetectable (Figure 5T–Y).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 5T-Y.

claim: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily localized in nuclei.
source: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily in nuclei while significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claim: Significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
source: TIR1-mCitrine is primarily in nuclei while significant amounts of AFB2 through AFB5 are present in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claim: AFB1-mCitrine appears primarily outside the nuclei.
source: Strikingly, AFB1-mCitrine appears primarily outside the nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and quantified in Figure 5S.

claim: TIR1 and AFB1 proteins exhibit contrasting patterns of primarily nuclear and cytoplasmic subcellular localizations, respectively.
source: Hence, despite being from the same clade, TIR1 and AFB1 proteins exhibit contrasting patterns of primarily nuclear and cytoplasmic subcellular localizations, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the localization data.

claim: Each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition.
source: The results in Figure 6 show that each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition but that, surprisingly, the afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin in the rapid root growth inhibition assay, indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
source: The results in Figure 6 show that each of the TIR1/AFBs contributes to rapid root growth inhibition but that, surprisingly, the afb1-3 mutant is almost completely resistant to auxin indicating that AFB1 is the dominant auxin receptor for this response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: Expression of AFB1-mCitrine under control of the AFB1 promoter restored the wild-level of auxin response in the rapid root growth inhibition assay.
source: Expression of AFB1-mCitrine under control of the AFB1 promoter restored the wild-level of auxin response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 6.

claim: The afb1 mutant is not affected in long-term inhibition of root growth.
source: This includes long-term inhibition of root growth.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of rapid and long-term assays.

claim: The afb1 mutant is a useful tool to discriminate between nongenomic and transcriptional auxin responses.
source: Thus, the afb1 mutant is a useful tool to discriminate between nongenomic and transcriptional auxin responses.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the differential effects of afb1 on rapid vs. long-term responses.

claim: The tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited a decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase compared to tir1afb345.
source: Strikingly, the tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited an additional decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase demonstrating that AFB1 is required for this phase (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: AFB1 is required for the initial lag phase of gravitropic response.
source: Strikingly, the tir1afb1345 mutant exhibited an additional decrease in the gravitropic response during the initial lag phase demonstrating that AFB1 is required for this phase (Figure 7A; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The tir1afb1 line showed a similar decrease in the lag phase of gravitropism compared to tir1.
source: The tir1afb1 line showed a similar decrease in the lag phase compared to tir1 (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TIR1 also contributes to the early gravitropic response since the tir1afb1 double mutant showed a stronger delay compared to either single mutant.
source: It seems likely that TIR1 also contributes to the early response since the tir1afb1 double mutant showed a stronger delay compared to either single mutant.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on comparison of gravitropism data.

claim: Both afb1 AFB1-mCitrine lines responded appreciably faster than the afb1 mutant during the first 2 hr of gravitropic response.
source: Further, both afb1 AFB1-mCitrine lines responded appreciably faster than the afb1 mutant during the first 2 hr with the brighter of the two mCitrine lines, line #7, exhibiting a difference by 30 min (Figure 7C; Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: AFB1 and the rapid response play a role at later stages of the gravitropic bending response.
source: Interestingly, both mCitrine lines started to plateau earlier and at a reduced angle compared to wild type while afb1 plateaued later and at an increased angle, suggesting that AFB1 and the rapid response also play a role at later stages of the gravitropic bending response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on gravitropism data.

claim: For most auxin-regulated growth processes, the TIR/AFB proteins retain largely overlapping functions despite diverging approximately 400 MYA.
source: Despite the fact that three major subclades were established approximately 400 MYA (Morris et al., 2018), our genetic studies reveal that for most auxin-regulated growth processes, the TIR/AFB proteins retain largely overlapping functions (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Morris et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 8.

claim: TIR1 is most important for normal growth and development among the TIR1/AFB proteins.
source: In general, TIR1 is most important for normal growth and development, but AFB5 and AFB2, and to a lesser extent AFB3 and AFB4, also play significant roles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the genetic analysis.

claim: TIR1 has a major role in the root while AFB5 is relatively more important in hypocotyl and inflorescence development.
source: Spatial differences are also apparent; TIR1 has a major role in the root while AFB5 is relatively more important in hypocotyl and inflorescence development.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on phenotypic analysis.

claim: The relative importance of individual TIR1/AFB proteins in various organs are at least partly related to differences in expression.
source: Although all six genes are broadly expressed, it appears that the relative importance of individual TIR1/AFB proteins in various organs are at least partly related to differences in expression.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on expression pattern analysis.

claim: AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence.
source: For example, AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence while in the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claim: In the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
source: For example, AFB5 is more broadly expressed than the other genes in the inflorescence while in the root, TIR1 and AFB2 are most highly expressed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claim: The AFB4 gene is expressed at a lower level in all tissues consistent with its relatively minor role.
source: The AFB4 gene is expressed at a lower level in all tissues consistent with its relatively minor role.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging and phenotypic analysis.

claim: The levels of the TIR1/AFB proteins are not uniform throughout the plant.
source: Our studies demonstrate that the levels of the TIR1/AFB proteins are not uniform throughout the plant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on fluorescence imaging.

claim: TIR1/AFB levels can be dynamic in a changing environment.
source: Earlier experiments also showed that TIR1/AFB levels can be dynamic in a changing environment (Vidal et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Vidal et al., 2010 and Wang et al., 2016.

claim: There is an asymmetric distribution of TIR1-mCitrine across flower primordia.
source: Given the debate over an auxin-response asymmetry across shoot organ primordia (Bhatia et al., 2019; Guan et al., 2019), it is particularly interesting that we see an asymmetric distribution of TIR1-mCitrine across flower primordia.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Bhatia et al., 2019 and Guan et al., 2019.

claim: The microRNA miR393 targets TIR1, AFB2, and AFB3 but not other members of the family.
source: For example, the microRNA miR393 is known to target TIR1, AFB2, and AFB3 but not other members of the family (Jones-Rhoades and Bartel, 2004; Navarro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Jones-Rhoades and Bartel, 2004 and Navarro et al., 2006.

claim: Regulation of miR393 abundance modulates the levels of TIR1, AFB2, and AFB3 to facilitate various growth processes in response to environmental signals.
source: Regulation of miR393 abundance modulates the levels of these three TIR1/AFBs to facilitate various growth processes, such as lateral root formation and hypocotyl elongation in response to environmental signals (Vidal et al., 2010; Pucciariello et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Vidal et al., 2010 and Pucciariello et al., 2018.

claim: Previous in vitro studies have documented some differences in the biochemical activity of members of the TIR1/AFB family.
source: Previous in vitro studies have documented some differences in the biochemical activity of members of the TIR1/AFB family (Calderón Villalobos et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Calderón Villalobos et al., 2012 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: An auxin-induced degradation assay in yeast reveals differences in the behavior of TIR1 and AFB2.
source: Similarly, an auxin-induced degradation assay in yeast reveals differences in the behavior of TIR1 and AFB2 (Wright et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Wright et al., 2017.

claim: The genetic results do not reveal any biochemical specificity among TIR1/AFB proteins, except for AFB1.
source: In contrast, our results do not reveal any biochemical specificity, except for AFB1 (see below).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the genetic analysis.

claim: The retention of overlapping functions among TIR1/AFB paralogs may reflect stricter constraints on TIR1/AFB protein function.
source: It is possible that the retention of overlapping functions reflects stricter constraints on TIR1/AFB protein function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: The different TIR1/AFB paralogs may have been maintained because they contribute to the robustness of the auxin signaling system.
source: One possibility is that the different TIR1/AFB paralogs have been maintained because they contribute to the robustness of the auxin signaling system.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: The importance of auxin in patterning of the developing embryo is well established.
source: The importance of auxin in patterning of the developing embryo is well established (Palovaara et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Palovaara et al., 2016.

claim: Auxin signaling is first apparent in the apical cell of the embryo.
source: Auxin signaling, as evidenced by activity of the DR5 reporter, is first apparent in the apical cell of the embryo (Friml et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Friml et al., 2003.

claim: The essential role of auxin in the apical cell and later in the hypophysis is clearly demonstrated by the defects in the division of these cells in the tir1afb235 quadruple and tir1afb12345 sextuple mutant.
source: The essential role of auxin in the apical cell and later in the hypophysis is clearly demonstrated by the defects in the division of these cells in the tir1afb235 quadruple and tir1afb12345 sextuple mutant (Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Similar embryo defects to those in tir1afb235 are observed in a number of other auxin mutants including those affecting response, auxin synthesis, and transport.
source: Similar defects are observed in a number of other auxin mutants including those affecting response (monopteros and bodenlos), auxin synthesis (yuc1 yuc4 yuc10 yuc11 and taa1 tar1 tar2) and transport (pin1 pin3 pin4 pin7 and aux1 lax1 lax2) (Berleth and Jürgens, 1993; Hardtke and Berleth, 1998; Hamann et al., 1999; Hamann et al., 2002; Friml et al., 2003; Cheng et al., 2007; Stepanova et al., 2008; Robert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with multiple citations.

claim: None of the other auxin mutants exhibit the fully penetrant embryo-lethal phenotype observed for the tir1afb235 quadruple and tir1afb12345 sextuple mutants.
source: However, none of these lines exhibit the fully penetrant embryo-lethal phenotype observed for the tir1afb235 quadruple and tir1afb12345 sextuple mutants.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on comparison with literature.

claim: Although tir1afb235 embryos form a morphologically normal hypophysis cell, this cell never expresses NTT-YPet or WOX5:GFP.
source: Although tir1afb235 embryos form a morphologically normal hypophysis cell, this cell never expresses NTT-YPet or WOX5:GFP.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on marker expression data.

claim: The proliferation of suspensor cells in the tir1afb235 mutant is associated with reduced expression of the suspensor marker PIN7-Venus and to a lesser extent NTT-YPet.
source: The proliferation of suspensor cells in the mutant is associated with reduced expression of the suspensor marker PIN7-Venus and to a lesser extent NTT-YPet suggesting that the TIR1/AFB pathway is required to maintain the suspensor cell fate, consistent with an earlier study (Rademacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Rademacher et al., 2012.

claim: The TIR1/AFB pathway is required to maintain the suspensor cell fate.
source: The proliferation of suspensor cells in the mutant is associated with reduced expression of the suspensor marker PIN7-Venus and to a lesser extent NTT-YPet suggesting that the TIR1/AFB pathway is required to maintain the suspensor cell fate, consistent with an earlier study (Rademacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Rademacher et al., 2012.

claim: PIN7 expression may normally be repressed in the embryo by a TIR1/AFB-dependent pathway.
source: It was surprising to observe that PIN7-Venus exhibits ectopic expression in the embryo proper. The reason for this is unclear but PIN7 expression may normally be repressed in the embryo by a TIR1/AFB-dependent pathway.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the ectopic expression data.

claim: The TIR1/AFB auxin receptors are not required for gametophyte development.
source: Our studies suggest that the TIR1/AFB auxin receptors are not required for gametophyte development although we cannot rule out a minor role.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on transmission rate data.

claim: It is possible that auxin is required in gametophytes but acts through a non-canonical pathway such as that involving auxin binding to the ETTIN protein.
source: Finally, it is possible that auxin is required, but acts through a non-canonical pathway such as that involving auxin binding to the ETTIN protein (Simonini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Simonini et al., 2016.

claim: AFB1 is unique among the auxin co-receptors and appears to have undergone pronounced functional changes during the diversification of the Brassicales order.
source: AFB1 is unique among the auxin co-receptors and appears to have undergone pronounced functional changes during the diversification of the Brasssicales order since the TIR1–AFB1 duplication in the At-β WGD around 80 to 90 million years ago (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Edger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to Edger et al., 2018.

claim: AFB1 can interact with Aux/IAA proteins in an auxin-dependent manner.
source: Although AFB1 can interact with Aux/IAA proteins in an auxin-dependent manner, it does not appear to assemble into a Skp, Cullin, F-box containing (SCF) complex as efficiently as the other TIR1/AFBs and is not primarily localized to the nucleus where it could directly influence transcriptional responses (Dharmasiri et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2015; Figure 5N and S; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Dharmasiri et al., 2005 and Yu et al., 2015, and reference to Figure 5.

claim: AFB1 does not appear to assemble into an SCF complex as efficiently as the other TIR1/AFBs.
source: Although AFB1 can interact with Aux/IAA proteins in an auxin-dependent manner, it does not appear to assemble into a Skp, Cullin, F-box containing (SCF) complex as efficiently as the other TIR1/AFBs and is not primarily localized to the nucleus where it could directly influence transcriptional responses (Dharmasiri et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2015; Figure 5N and S; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Dharmasiri et al., 2005 and Yu et al., 2015, and reference to Figure 5.

claim: AFB1 is not primarily localized to the nucleus where it could directly influence transcriptional responses.
source: Although AFB1 can interact with Aux/IAA proteins in an auxin-dependent manner, it does not appear to assemble into a Skp, Cullin, F-box containing (SCF) complex as efficiently as the other TIR1/AFBs and is not primarily localized to the nucleus where it could directly influence transcriptional responses (Dharmasiri et al., 2005; Yu et al., 2015; Figure 5N and S; Figure 5—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Dharmasiri et al., 2005 and Yu et al., 2015, and reference to Figure 5.

claim: The F-Box substitutions in AFB1 affecting SCF assembly appeared between approximately 45 and 65 million years ago.
source: The F-Box substitutions in AFB1 affecting SCF assembly appeared between approximately 45 and 65 million years ago (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C; Edger et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and citation to Edger et al., 2018.

claim: Unlike the other TIR1/AFB genes that are broadly expressed in most cells, AFB1 is expressed very highly in some tissues (root epidermis and vascular tissue) and not at all in others (meristematic pericycle and early embryos).
source: It is noteworthy that unlike the other TIR1/AFB genes that are broadly expressed in most cells, AFB1 is expressed very highly in some tissues (root epidermis and vascular tissue) and not at all in others (meristematic pericycle and early embryos).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on expression pattern data.

claim: AFB1 appears to have a negative effect on lateral root initiation in the afb234 and afb345 lines.
source: Based on our genetic studies, AFB1 appears to have a negative effect on lateral root initiation in the afb234 and afb345 lines despite the fact that AFB1 is not expressed in the pericycle, the site of lateral root initiation, suggesting that this may be a non-cell-autonomous effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on genetic data.

claim: AFB1's negative effect on lateral root initiation may be a non-cell-autonomous effect.
source: Based on our genetic studies, AFB1 appears to have a negative effect on lateral root initiation in the afb234 and afb345 lines despite the fact that AFB1 is not expressed in the pericycle, the site of lateral root initiation, suggesting that this may be a non-cell-autonomous effect.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on the expression pattern.

claim: AFB2 through AFB5 are distributed between the nucleus and the cytoplasm in epidermal cells of the root.
source: We find that AFB2 through AFB5 are distributed between the nucleus and the cytoplasm, at least in epidermal cells of the root (Figure 5S).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with reference to Figure 5S.

claim: The paralogs TIR1 and AFB1 differ dramatically in being highly enriched in the nucleus and in the cytoplasm, respectively.
source: In contrast, the paralogs TIR1 and AFB1 differ dramatically in being highly enriched in the nucleus and in the cytoplasm, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on localization data.

claim: Auxin treatment results in very rapid responses in Arabidopsis roots including increased cytosolic Ca++ levels, alkalinization of the apoplast and inhibition of root growth.
source: In Arabidopsis roots, auxin treatment results in very rapid responses including increased cytosolic Ca++ levels, alkalinization of the apoplast and inhibition of root growth (Shih et al., 2015; Dindas et al., 2018; Fendrych et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Shih et al., 2015, Dindas et al., 2018, and Fendrych et al., 2018.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated that two rapid responses, inhibition of root growth and membrane depolarization in root hairs, do require the TIR1/AFBs.
source: However, recent studies have demonstrated that two rapid responses, inhibition of root growth and membrane depolarization in root hairs, do require the TIR1/AFBs (Dindas et al., 2018; Fendrych et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Dindas et al., 2018 and Fendrych et al., 2018.

claim: The rapid growth inhibition response is mediated primarily by AFB1.
source: Surprisingly we find that the growth inhibition response is mediated primarily by AFB1.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on the rapid root growth inhibition data.

claim: AFB1's role in rapid growth inhibition may reflect the high level of AFB1 in the cytoplasm.
source: This may reflect the high level of AFB1 in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation based on localization data.

claim: It is possible that AFB1's specialization is a relatively recent event and that the responsibility of mediating the rapid response is shared by multiple TIR1/AFB proteins in other plant lineages.
source: It is possible that AFB1's specialization is a relatively recent event and that the responsibility of mediating the rapid response is shared by multiple TIR1/AFB proteins in other plant lineages.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation.

claim: The rapid nongenomic auxin response in the Arabidopsis root has a role in early stages of root gravitropism.
source: It has been proposed that the rapid nongenomic auxin response in the Arabidopsis root has a role in early stages of root gravitropism (Sato et al., 2015), and our results support this idea.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Sato et al., 2015.

claim: The afb1 mutation confers a clear decrease in early gravity response in combination with tir1 or tir1afb345.
source: Although the afb1 mutant has only a modest effect on gravitropism by itself, in combination with tir1 or tir1afb345, it confers a clear decrease in early gravity response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section based on gravitropism data.

claim: The rapid auxin response is probably not unique to the Brassicales given that a relatively fast gravitropic response is common in diverse seed plants.
source: Although the rapid auxin response has only been described thus far in Arabidopsis, it is probably not unique to the Brassicales given that a relatively fast gravitropic response is common in diverse seed plants (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: If the rapid auxin response evolved prior to the TIR1–AFB1 duplication event and the ancestral TIR1/AFBs contributed to both the nuclear genomic and cytoplasmic nongenomic auxin responses, the differences between TIR1 and AFB1 represent an elegant example of subfunctionalization.
source: If the rapid auxin response evolved prior to the TIR1–AFB1 duplication event and the ancestral TIR1/AFBs contributed to both the nuclear genomic and cytoplasmic nongenomic auxin responses, the differences between TIR1 and AFB1 represent an elegant example of subfunctionalization of AFB1 to a role in the non-genomic response and, possibly, of TIR1 to specialize in the nuclear auxin response.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as speculation about evolutionary history.

claim: The afb1 mutant provides a useful tool to separate genomic and non-genomic auxin responses.
source: Furthermore, as AFB1 has a major role in the rapid response but little or no function in the transcriptional response, the afb1 mutant provides a useful tool to separate the two responses.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion from the functional analysis.

claim: The TIR1/AFB genes likely evolved from a gene encoding an F-Box/LRR protein similar to those present in the genomes of extant streptophyte algae.
source: As shown earlier (Hori et al., 2014; Mutte et al., 2018), the TIR1/AFB genes likely evolved from a gene encoding an F-Box/LRR protein similar to those present in the genomes of extant streptophyte algae.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Hori et al., 2014 and Mutte et al., 2018.

claim: Algal F-Box/LRR proteins form a sister clade to three distinct land plant F-Box families: the TIR1/AFB auxin receptors, the COI1 jasmonate-Ile receptors, and the 'XFB' clade.
source: These algal proteins form a sister clade to three distinct land plant F-Box families, the TIR1/AFB auxin receptors, the COI1 jasmonate-Ile (or dinor-OPDA) receptors, and the 'XFB' clade of unknown function conserved in the genomes of mosses and some lycophytes but not in other land plants (Prigge et al., 2010; Bowman et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to Prigge et al., 2010 and Bowman et al., 2019.

claim: The last common ancestors of land plants and of vascular plants had only one TIR1/AFB gene.
source: While the last common ancestors of land plants and of vascular plants had only one TIR1/AFB gene, three clades of auxin receptors were established prior to the radiation of euphyllophytes (ferns plus seed plants) over 400 million years ago (Morris et al., 2018; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citation to Morris et al., 2018 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A gene duplication event prior to angiosperm radiation split the TIR1/AFB1 clade from the AFB2/AFB3 clade.
source: Another gene duplication event prior to angiosperm radiation split the TIR1/AFB1 clade from the AFB2/AFB3 clade.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section based on phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Both the AFB2/AFB3 and the AFB4/AFB5 duplication events coincide with the At-α WGD prior to divergence of the Brassicaceae family.
source: The gene duplication event establishing the distinct TIR1 and AFB1 clades is coincident with the At-β WGD event at the base of Brassicales, while both the AFB2/AFB3 and the AFB4/AFB5 duplication events coincide with the more recent At-α WGD prior to divergence of the Brassicaceae family (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A; Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Schranz and Mitchell-Olds, 2006.
